items.summary: Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said on Nov 17 that he wanted his job back, despite resigning over an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. In his first statement since stepping down last week, Huang wrote: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO." He added that if the Board decides his return serves shareholders, employees, the company, and America, he would be honored to come back. The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia, which lost US$700 billion (S$902 billion) in market value since it broke; Huang is set to face questions from US lawmakers on Dec 1 over national security concerns. His fall triggered calls for his return from Elon Musk and other entrepreneurs, and President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at Nvidia while downplaying the spy allegations. On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions on AI chip exports that drew condemnation from Beijing, just as talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping were set to begin this week at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Under the new rules, data centres worldwide will need a US licence to supply large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau, or other countries under US arms embargoes; licences are also required to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil over diversion risk. The changes target a loophole that let Chinese firms rent AI computing power from data centres abroad running on US hardware not available for export to China. Huang's lover Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud firm under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia chips in circumvention of export controls; she is unrelated to the 63-year-old chief. Nvidia's Nov 17 third-quarter results, scheduled for 5pm ET (6am on Nov 18 in Singapore), will be the first presented by interim CEO Colette Kress. Jacob Bourne of Emarketer said a business-as-usual tone from her would likely not be well received; analysts expect scrutiny over whether she will slow Huang's aggressive investment strategy, Nvidia's future sales guidance, and its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. The situation carries wider stakes: Nvidia backs major labs including Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Nov 19. AFP reported that Huang sounded contrition in his statement, saying "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life."
items.title: Jensen Huang seeks return as Nvidia prepares first earnings since scandal and new US chip curbs

items.summary: At the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday, Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, its next major server operating system release. The version ships by default with a hardened Server Core configuration and a new security baseline that lets administrators relax specific settings to reduce the effort of establishing secure defaults from day one, according to Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM. Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines to guarantee boot integrity across a VM fleet, while Confidential VM support begins a journey toward supporting integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware. The hardened settings span identity and authentication (Kerberos over NTLM, protected LSASS, strong passwords with account lockout, no consumer accounts), network exposure (SMB signing and encryption, firewall enabled in every profile, legacy name resolution and unauthenticated RPC disabled), cryptography (TLS limited to modern cipher suites, hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange, strongly protected stored keys), privilege and admin access (admins approve elevation, powerful rights retained by Administrators, guests cannot sign in, installers cannot self-elevate), platform and code integrity (sign-in runs only Microsoft-signed code, stricter signature validation, encrypted paging file), and remote access and observability (RDP with NLA and TLS, WinRM without Basic/Digest/unencrypted traffic, advanced audit with command lines, PowerShell script block logging, larger event logs). The company noted it is still working on NTLM blocking, hardware-backed platform protection, print and RPC hardening, and additional settings among the hundreds enabled from first boot. Windows Server 2028 also brings simplified management at scale through Intune for eligible persistent servers covering configuration, compliance, applications, and updates; performance improvements via native NVMe storage by default, NVMe over TCP and RDMA transports, and ReFS boot support; and new AI accelerators to deploy and configure inference environments, manage accelerated hardware, and support open-weight and custom models including Windows ML, Foundry Local, vLLM, and Llama.cpp. Administrators can test the release through the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access. Hinnant described the release as raising the security and access bar, accelerating enterprise infrastructure, simplifying management at scale, and beginning long-term investments extending Microsoft Foundry toward local token factories that give customers more choices on intelligence placement and cost structure. The article concludes with an unrelated advertisement for Adaptive Security's AI agents analyzing email intent to detect phishing, business email compromise, and invoice fraud via a 14-day read-only scan of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace without MX changes.
items.title: Microsoft Announces Windows Server 2028 with Hardened Security and AI Accelerators

items.summary: General Motors has begun rolling out the Apple Wallet digital-key feature to select models from its Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC brands. Eligible customers will receive notifications in the “What’s New” section of their vehicle’s app when digital-key support becomes available for a given model, with more vehicles expected to be added over time. Supported drivers can use their smartphones or Apple Watches as keys to unlock their vehicles, mirroring how a physical key would function. GM states that eligible supported vehicles will automatically unlock as the driver approaches and lock as the driver walks away. The company also reports that the vehicle’s trunk and climate control system become accessible through the new feature. In a press release, GM said: “The digital key experience will continue to evolve beyond simply unlocking and starting a vehicle.” It added that by leveraging ultra-wideband technology, GM is laying the groundwork for more deeply integrated experiences such as automatically adjusting vehicle settings as drivers approach, along with other intelligent features designed to make ownership more convenient. Apple first announced the concept at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2020, and it later launched exclusively for select 2021 BMW 5 Series models before expanding to automakers including Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, and Audi. Regarding functionality without power, the company said that depending on a user’s iPhone model, keys could remain available even when a device needs charging; however, it warned such availability would be limited to up to five hours. The article notes this development follows Samsung rolling out its own version of digital keys in 2021 and announcing support for select GM vehicles in October. As first reported by MacRumors, the rollout is described as only the beginning of a broader evolution toward more integrated experiences. It should be noted that specific supported models are not enumerated in the report beyond Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC brands generally.
items.title: GM Rolls Out Apple Wallet Digital Keys to Cadillac, Chevrolet and GMC Vehicles

items.summary: A letter to a Singapore forum titled 'Carpark gantry reliability must match new payment transitions' argues that the ongoing phasing out of the NETS CashCard by December 31 requires dependable ground infrastructure, since many drivers have already faced frustration with carpark gantries failing to detect stored-value cards. The author recounts being trapped at a Gombak carpark gantry behind a queue of more than 10 vehicles after his EZ-Link card was not read. His initial intercom calls went unanswered; when an operator finally responded, she dismissively claimed the EZ-Link card was not accepted despite his regular use there and hung up after stating she could not raise the barrier remotely. A callback offered only a suggestion to make a U-turn, which he said was impossible given cars hemmed in behind and beside him. He had to repeatedly reverse and inch forward in a tight space, risking scraping the gantry or hitting the car behind. The reader eventually detected his card, leading him to conclude that the sensor quality of the gantry was at fault rather than any problem with the card. The author contends that recurring gantry glitches create safety hazards, bottlenecks, and undue stress for drivers, and urges authorities to hold carpark operators accountable for gantry maintenance and responsive support before enforcing further card phase-outs. The piece is signed by Lim Kien Mau and references a related article dated November 16 about switching from the NETS CashCard before January 1, 2027, for ERP and parking payments.
items.title: Motorist urges accountability for unreliable carpark gantries amid payment card phase-out

items.summary: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027, with South and South-east Asia as key priorities. The announcement came from S.B. Seker, Binance's regional business head for APAC, who spoke at the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov 18, not long after the firm was hit by a record US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) digital heist in October. Seker told Reuters that Binance has ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets, three of which are in quite mature stages, while the others remain in early discussions. He did not specify which new markets were being considered, though Binance currently holds operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions. Details of the planned expansion are expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of 2027. The expansion plans follow a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from Binance's platform in October. Both the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, though Pyongyang has denied involvement. Experts describe the heist as the largest crypto theft ever, which has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices across the industry. In response to the incident, Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November after covering 95% of the lost tokens, and last weekend aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of that week. Seker noted that within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. He added there was no single country leading the charge in investigations, though Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry overall. As he put it: 'this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat,' reflecting a shift from addressing the original incident toward how the entire ecosystem prepares for such risks going forward. Seker emphasized that while Binance remains part of this conversation, it is no longer driving it in isolation. Reuters reported on these developments; all figures are as stated by the source item. items.summary: The author distinguishes two separate takeaways from the recent METR (Machine Intelligence Research Institute) report: that AI will soon fully automate AI research, and that an intelligence explosion has become more plausible. The first is described as a strong update toward shorter timelines; taking the report at face value, AI is already causing much more of a speedup in AI R&D than expected and improving at a faster rate, so full automation appears closer and moving faster (with some nuance about whether this stems from stronger coding uplift, better R&D performance, or something else). The second takeaway is assessed as only a moderate update toward an intelligence explosion. The key question is whether the feedback loop of AI improving itself can accelerate over time even holding compute fixed: higher effective capability index (ECI) leads to more AI R&D labour, which increases total R&D effort, which raises ECI again. Stage 1—higher ECI producing more quality-adjusted AI R&D labour—is judged much stronger than before; during the relevant period ECI scores rose by about two years' worth of progress while generating far less extra labour than expected. Stage 2—the extent to which improved labour can substitute for increased compute and labour in total effort—is assessed as only slightly stronger, because Anthropic's progress sped up roughly 2x (mostly attributed to AI) even though training-compute growth did not speed up; this weakens the most extreme bottleneck view but does not rule out more moderate views that compute caps acceleration at several times today's pace. It also leaves open whether much algorithmic progress depends on scale-dependent algorithms, which would slow progress without larger training scales (though METR reported no significant bottlenecks over the next 12 months, with limited confidence and redacted analysis of specific bottlenecks). Stage 3—more total R&D effort producing higher ECI—is judged a bit stronger; some recent speedup was not driven by increased AI R&D inputs but by progress being easier to make (with METR attributing non-AI factors in late 2025, though redacting details), and doubling AI R&D inputs produced more progress than expected. The author notes that the more sceptical one is about stage 1, the more one should update upward on stage 3: once faster progress is accepted, at least one stage must be updated unless non-AI inputs such as hiring or experiment compute also sped up significantly (with a '2025' date associated with this claim). Overall, the author concludes that there is definite evidence of accelerating progress but not overwhelming evidence; it could still go either way. The author feels less bullish than AIFP and notes that even without accelerating progress, AI progress will become much faster if AI R&D is automated.
items.title: METR report implies both shorter timelines and a more likely intelligence explosion

items.summary: According to The Wall Street Journal, the Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil investigation into Nvidia over whether the company's disclosures misled investors. This probe arrives as CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export laws. Congress has separately demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his position advocating for loosened export restrictions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Nvidia over the weekend of knowingly selling powerful chips to China 'to goose their revenues and their earnings.' The SEC probe coincides with Nvidia's reported earnings in a market where its stock has fallen more than 10% since Huang departed; the company reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago. items.summary:
Tyler Buchanan, a 24-year-old from Dundee, has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the United States after conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies through text message phishing and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims. Prosecutors described the thefts as having 'severe, life-altering consequences' for victims and highlighted them as evidence of the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

Buchanan began hacking as a teenager and was part of Scattered Spider, a collective of young hackers blamed for numerous high-profile cyber-crimes. He admitted taking part in a campaign that started in 2021 when he was 19. Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers based in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

The group sent hundreds of SMS messages to mobile phones belonging to workers at large tech or telecoms firms. The phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to resemble legitimate sites of victim companies, using text such as 'Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps'. These websites lured recipients into providing confidential information including personal identifying information (PII), usernames and passwords. Buchanan set up a Telegram bot to collect all victims' credentials.

For some victim companies, stolen data included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers. The group then used this stolen information along with SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States. In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

The scheme made them $8m in less than two years according to US prosecutors. Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals. In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency. Cyber security researchers and journalists reported he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch, as noted by Unit221B researcher Allison Nixon.

Buchanan reportedly fled to Canada before returning home. In April 2023 officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI, recovering a device containing names and addresses of hacking victims along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim. The following month he left the UK again.

He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples, then extradited to the United States where he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to Scattered Spider. They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail. Two other members of the group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused £39m of damage.
items.title: British hacker Tyler Buchanan jailed six years in US for $11.6m text-message phishing scheme

items.summary: Anton Osika, CEO of Lovable, a generative-AI startup recently valued at over $13 billion and flush with investment cash after two years, is shifting the platform's focus beyond helping users build apps toward enabling them to earn money from those projects. The company reports that around 80 percent of users arrive seeking a financial incentive, such as building customer-facing platforms for online sales, yet only 35 percent currently earn revenue from their work. Osika frames this gap with the question of whether someone who likes cakes could vibe-code a living out of it—illustrating his goal of helping people run small businesses based on passions, like opening a cake shop. Cofounder and chief technology officer Fabian Hedin says Lovable is building automations to support everything from initial business strategy and website creation to long-term customer retention and marketing plans; for example, a cake shop owner would receive an AI-generated morning briefing through a chatbot-style dashboard that analyzes sales of cake boxes during holiday promotions, automatically answers customer emails, and reminds the owner to make financial deposits on time. Osika notes that vibe-coded projects have been especially valuable to social media content creators who can leverage their platforms better through sites built with Lovable, building larger businesses around their audiences—examples include a creator using it to sell their book and others selling merchandise. The startup faces an uphill battle earning the trust of these entrepreneurs because vibe-coded projects were notorious for security flaws that exposed user data on the open web; earlier this month Lovable revamped its security approach as part of making sites generated through its platform more secure by default. Igor Andriushchenko, Lovable's head of security, told WIRED: "The moment real people use what you build, security is the product." Osika will consider next year a success if he can help a new wave of entrepreneurs start sustainable businesses—"Why just vibe code an app when you can vibe code a living?"
items.title: Lovable Pivots to Help Users Vibe-Code Sustainable Businesses Amid Security Overhaul

items.summary: A collaboration between Inside Climate News (ICN) and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette built an interactive map that lets anyone search any location in Pennsylvania for nearby oil and gas wells, many of which are long forgotten or abandoned. The tool pulls data from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), which is responsible for its accuracy; residents with concerns can contact the agency directly through a form or by calling their local oil and gas office. ICN simplified DEP well-status descriptions into four categories: Active/Other, mostly wells still producing oil or gas under a regulatory inactive status that lets an operator shut down production for up to five years without sealing a well; Plugged (recorded as sealed), which were plugged either by contractors hired by former operators or by the state, though plugging can fail and some may still leak gases; Abandoned/Orphaned, covering wells out of production for more than 12 months plus orphaned wells with no responsible owner; and Historical, drawn from DEP’s digitizing historical maps that are not comprehensive and have largely not been verified by modern inspections. The map centers on Brittany and Ryan Mahoney in the South Fayette neighborhood known as The Berkshires, where six old oil wells sit within 150 feet of their first home—none of which they knew about. Their original house sat near a well that was reportedly capped before construction began; DEP records show no such work occurred, though historic maps indicate two oil wells were drilled less than 50 feet from where a trampoline now stands in the Mahoneys’ backyard, and a recent visit found no visible evidence of any well. A neighbor two houses down reported having no nearby wells, yet the map shows otherwise; Agnes Warner’s own home is among six on her street marked by old-well dots. The Berkshires was once part of the McDonald Oil Field, one of the most prolific oil plays in the world at the time. In southwestern Pennsylvania residents could have dozens of such dots near their homes. Many abandoned or orphaned wells pose no obvious danger, but Dan Brockett, who leads Penn State Extension’s energy education team and spent much of last year hunting old wells with his wife for an Environmental Defense Fund–funded effort, says leaks are the biggest concern—whether methane, brine water, or petroleum products—and should be reported to the DEP. He also warns that severe erosion can create sinkholes, and that cut-off surface pipes or rusty pipe sticking out pose tripping hazards; he advises against cutting or pulling old pipes because they may trap methane. Brockett’s fieldwork found about 250 wells the DEP did not know about—a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands suspected in Pennsylvania. He noted many sites showed erosion or water running through them, likely indicating corroded casing, and that leaking gas often carried a slight petroleum odor with dead vegetation around the well head even though pure methane is odorless. The article cautions against dangerous DIY tests like holding a lit match to a source or capturing emissions in a makeshift canister, since captured methane could explode if it finds a spark; methane venting into air is not necessarily hazardous on its own. If residents smell gas near their home, the odorant utilities inject may be responsible rather than an old well—in that case they should call their natural gas utility immediately and leave the house while waiting for a sensor check. Gas becomes explosive between 5% and 15% of air volume in a room; below or above that it will not ignite, though utilities typically shut off supply at even half a percent level before determining the cause. Fred Baldassare, who has investigated leaking methane for more than three decades—first as a DEP stray gas investigator and now with his firm Echelon Applied Geochemistry Consulting—is said to have thousands of photos documenting leak effects on homes, from bubbling water wells to rubble after explosions. He says the most common way methane issues surface is through gas utility surveys: companies like Columbia Gas or Peoples in southwestern Pennsylvania survey pipelines for leaks, and if detected gas does not match their pipeline’s chemical signature they notify the DEP, which launches an investigation. The state may fail to find a source, or determine plugging would be too disruptive—such as when a leaking well was found in the floor of Braddock’s 1889 Carnegie Library building—and instead install mitigation systems that dig trenches around or inside ground floors and direct gas away from homes; Baldassare has installed dozens. The DEP also installs vents directly on abandoned wells, some later plugged, to route gas to the atmosphere rather than into enclosed spaces where it could collect—done about two dozen times, mostly in southwestern Pennsylvania. Residents are encouraged to report suspected undocumented wells via a form requesting contact information, location, whether it is visibly leaking, photos and GPS coordinates; Brockett advises standing at the site for several minutes to let GPS calibrate before pulling coordinates. The DEP will determine ownership and classify a well as abandoned (operator still responsible) or orphaned (no owner, becoming a ward of the state), noting that merely finding a buried well does not make landowners liable—though producing it, receiving economic benefit, improperly discarding evidence, or other careless acts can create financial responsibility. The DEP prioritizes plugging by risk and plugs only a handful per year on an emergency basis; absent immediate hazard, remediation could take years. Pamela Schrank’s Murrysville home became prominent in spring 2024 when she grew dizzy from odor coming from an abandoned well while gardening and reported it to the DEP. Rep. Summer Lee visited the Westmoreland County home and cited it in Washington testimony; funding for plugging had been held up by the Trump administration as part of President Joe Biden’s Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act before being released, yet two and a half years later Schrank said the well was still leaking with an ephemeral gas smell within 10-15 feet that comes and goes in waves. If classified orphaned, plugging becomes the agency’s responsibility; if abandoned with a known owner, the DEP tries to force that owner to plug it rather than shift burden to taxpayers—a process that could take years or not happen at all. The largest operating owner of abandoned wells in Pennsylvania is Alabama-based Diversified Energy Co., which has thousands of wells required to be plugged under consent agreements spreading responsibility over 15 years. Old wells can also suddenly become problems: Baldassare recalled a long-dormant well outside a Fox Chapel home that one morning dumped mud and soil on the front window, possibly from corroded casing failure or underground pressure shifts, with mining activity able to shift subsurface pressure too. Because of infrastructure density and links between wells and geological layers in southwestern Pennsylvania, plugging one well—or drilling/fracking new ones—can cause others to develop problems; shale developers must notify the DEP of “communication” incidents where their activity is suspected to impact another well. Of 60 reported incidents to date, most come to light when other operators detect pressure changes and notify the active-frack company—but this could also be happening at unmonitored abandoned or orphaned wells. One such case involved a New Freeport (Greene County) well that activated with gas and liquid in 2022 while EQT Corp. fracked about a mile away; EQT reported it but now believes the timing was coincident and denies a link, though local residents drawing aquifer water believe their abandoned-well activity affected it and have filed a lawsuit after township supervisors declared a state of emergency to build a municipal water line. The piece closes by noting what lies underground is also regional history: signs at McDonald Trail Station and History Center suggest as many as 200 wells once stood within McDonald Borough during the brief, spectacular 19th-century oil boom; photos in Tim Thomassy’s basement collection depict derricks from that era.
items.title: Pennsylvania residents may live near abandoned oil and gas wells with no easy way to know

items.summary: Inside Climate News partnered with the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette to build a streamlined, responsive mapping tool that helps residents identify abandoned oil and gas wells near their homes, schools, workplaces, and parks. The project grew out of Allegheny County research using an interactive map, which led reporters to South Fayette Township's Berkshires neighborhood—where homeowners were unaware that hundreds of old wells lay beneath new suburban developments, marked by purple dots in the tool. Pennsylvania's geology is described as resembling a block of Swiss cheese due to decades of drilling; since Edwin Drake struck oil less than 70 feet below the surface near Titusville in 1859 through to the fracking boom that began in 2004, hundreds of thousands of wells have been drilled into the region. Many are now abandoned and often invisible at the surface—hidden in forests, shopping centers, even beneath the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden and the terminal runways of Pittsburgh International Airport—and could lie under a resident's own home or backyard. While most pose little hazard beyond tripping over pipes, some may leak explosive methane, toxic carbon monoxide, or carcinogens like benzene, creating air and water pollution; residents are advised to exercise great care if they suspect a nearby well. The state Department of Environmental Protection offers an oil and gas well mapping tool, but the collaboration created their version because it can be slow and difficult for non-experts to use. They simplified the agency's classification into four categories: Active/Other (mostly producing wells or those in regulatory inactive status allowing shutdowns up to five years without sealing), Plugged/sealed wells (recorded as sealed by contractors or state, though plugging may fail over time as metal and cement deteriorate), Abandoned/Orphaned (out of production more than 12 months; orphaned means no responsible operator exists), and Historical (from maps the DEP is digitizing that cover only southwest Pennsylvania so far and have largely not been verified by modern inspections, requiring extra caution). Wells appearing as proposed but never drilled were excluded. The tool lets users type an address or accept suggestions, zooms to display well information including distance from the searched location, and offers a 'See photos' button for available government inspection images. Data limitations are acknowledged: the DEP is responsible for accuracy, so concerns should be directed through their form or oil and gas office; wells may appear in both historical maps and the active inventory, may be duplicated across two digitized collections with slightly different locations, and can be misclassified—such as Jane McGill #1 on the Botanic Garden property, listed as 'active' at publication but actually abandoned. Only agency-mapped wells were included, so many older wells (possibly several hundred thousand) remain unmapped; more than 29,000 wells with no coordinates in the inventory could not be mapped—about half Plugged, almost 6,000 Abandoned/Orphaned, and the remainder Active/Other. Residents are warned that a clean map result does not guarantee absence of nearby wells, noting signs like dead vegetation, bubbling water, rusted equipment, sinkholes, or petroleum smells; reporting concerns requires GPS coordinates to prioritize environmental or safety risks, with 'direct threats' to homes, schools, or public spaces eligible for immediate plugging under emergency contracts. Penn State University offers well-water testing for drilling pollution, and the map was built using free, open-source software documented in a GitHub repository containing technical details, code, and full methods.
items.title: How and Why We Mapped Pennsylvania's Forgotten Oil and Gas Wells

items.summary: On November 6, 2024, Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) introduced a regulatory framework to promote the integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) with existing solar photovoltaic installations. The guidelines establish a competitive bidding and capacity allocation mechanism for eligible grid-connected PV plants exceeding 1 MW in size. Successful applicants must install battery storage with a minimum energy capacity equivalent to 2.61 MWh per MW of rated storage power, complete installation and grid connection within 15 months, and release grid connection capacity equal to 1.5 times the rated storage power. The framework also includes provisions for a daily guaranteed billing quantity linked to 2.61 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to operational requirements. Electricity discharge will be coordinated according to national utility Taipower's scheduling and dispatch needs, shifting part of Taiwan's solar output from midday periods toward times when stored energy provides greater value. The competitive bidding mechanism determines battery capacity tariffs offered to successful applicants, introducing market-based price competition intended to improve grid infrastructure utilization and enable additional renewable integration. In January 2025, MOEA announced plans to accelerate solar and offshore wind deployment targeting an additional 8.2 GW of combined capacity by end of 2026, though deployment has progressed more slowly than anticipated. A December 2025 GlobalData forecast projected Taiwan's cumulative solar capacity would reach 31.2 GW by 2035, with the 20 GW milestone now expected in 2029; the government maintained solar feed-in tariffs for 2026 at levels set in the second half of 2025 to sustain investment and deployment. Energy storage is gaining prominence: French manufacturer Saft announced plans in October 2025 to supply 356 MWh for a Taichung project, bringing its planned installed capacity on the island to 630 MWh by 2026. Earlier examples of storage integration include a 15 MW/15 MWh battery system connected to a 150 MW solar park in southern Taiwan.
items.title: Taiwan introduces bidding framework for storage deployment at existing PV plants

items.summary: Mitch Hall and his wife Lori live in one of a few dozen town houses built so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes there produce roughly as much solar energy as they consume, storing surplus power in batteries for evening use. In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in what will become Michigan's first residential virtual power plant (VPP) pilot; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy would then remotely control residents' home batteries to inject stored solar onto the grid when operators need it most. Joi Harris, president and CEO of DTE Energy, said in a statement that 'this pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,' noting VPPs can smooth demand peaks and reduce reliance on expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants and grid-infrastructure upgrades. Residents would also be compensated: Matt Hall said DTE 'will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.' The utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and prices are likely highest, so residents need not optimize usage themselves; however, exact compensation figures were unavailable because DTE did not respond to Canary Media's request in time for publication. VPPs have existed for years but gained traction slowly due to lack of utility incentives and high costs of home solar and batteries, though electrification and a data center rush are now driving demand growth. Earlier this month the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources in VPPs could save households an average of $122 per year by 2050. Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI, said 'there's immense untapped capacity.' Matt Grocoff, founder of Thrive Collaborative, began considering a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019 to mimic an ecosystem where homes produce their own energy and share it mutually across a network rather than through a one-directional grid; he described how each home 'can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy.' DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to participate, with the pilot expected to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units without batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA supplies the home storage systems and is helping DTE operate the pilot using its proprietary software; Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA's VPP business unit, called Veridian 'a test bed.' He pointed to a similar Sonnen-facilitated program that began in 2017 at Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City with solar on a new apartment building. Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission extended the initial program to every residential customer after promising early data; today about 7,900 homes and businesses participate under the name Wattsmart Battery across Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho. Brehm would like more utilities to launch at full scale given numerous existing programs to model on, but noted Rocky Mountain Power's pilot is a good example for cautious utilities because its employees quickly understood how the residential battery fleet works and could integrate it into operations and resource-capacity planning; he'd like DTE to do likewise. The Veridian VPP pilot has already inspired developers and utilities outside Michigan, including Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, according to Grocoff, who said 'we're getting calls from all over the country.'
items.title: Veridian at County Farm to become Michigan's first virtual power plant pilot

items.summary: The article centers on how climate change is making app-based delivery work in New York City increasingly dangerous, while documenting the workers' own organizing to improve their conditions. José Yos, a 40-year-old Guatemalan food-and-grocery deliverista who rides e-bikes for apps like DoorDash (element_id: entity-502-510), describes riding through wildfire smoke from Quebec wildfires in Canada on sweltering days during the city's second heat emergency of two weeks, when temperatures were projected to reach close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit with an even higher heat index. He wore a balaclava and kept working because he had reserved his Uber Eats hours ahead and feared losing his rating or being deactivated if deliveries slowed (element_id: entity-1364-1373). Before the city's deactivation protection bill enacted in January 2026, workers could be removed from apps without cause; now apps must give 72 hours' notice before deactivating a worker and have the action investigated. Yos nonetheless avoided triggering that process (element_id: date-1611-1615). He said weather affects him in two ways — risking health and safety while putting his livelihood on the line, since apps do not grant extra time to pick up or drop off orders when conditions are bad, which lowers ratings. Of roughly 70,000 delivery workers across the five boroughs (element_id: quantity-3412-3427), many hail from Latin America, with a growing number being migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — regions facing climate change's brunt; Guatemala has suffered droughts and flooding that suppressed crop yields, linked to both climate change and El Niño patterns. As gig-economy freelancers, these workers lack adequate health and safety protections.
items.title: Climate change intensifies dangers for New York's migrant delivery workers amid labor organizing and adaptation efforts

The Senate is poised to pass a "permitting reform" bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which would streamline federal permit processes for large infrastructure projects. The motivation stems from delays that have slowed renewable energy development: the SunZia wind farm transmission line in New Mexico, described as the largest renewable project ever built in the United States, took two decades to construct and remains entangled in unresolved court battles over impacts on historic sites even after completion in June. Such legal challenges are said to threaten long-distance power line construction nationwide.

At its core, BAAJA would speed up environmental and historic preservation reviews under laws including the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) and the National Historic Preservation Act by narrowing what agencies must consider, restricting who can sue over those reviews, and shortening deadlines. Companies argue permits are time-consuming, unpredictable, and costly; opponents say this reduces public scrutiny and makes it harder for communities and tribes to identify harms or protect sacred sites.

The bill also targets the power grid specifically: giving federal authorities greater ability to override states that block interstate lines, requiring regional operators to approve reliability-improving lines, and preventing states from using the Clean Water Act to block crossings unless they directly discharge into water. It would not affect most projects on private land within one state.

On communities, experts expect reduced power for tribes, states, and local groups to delay or scrutinize projects, alongside slightly lower electricity costs over 15 years as cheap regional power moves more easily and rooftop solar sales improve. Most data centers are expected to see little change because they sit on private land under state oversight; the bill could still accelerate their supporting infrastructure while requiring them to pay for grid upgrades and increasing transparency around electricity use.

On climate, BAAJA would enable both fossil fuel and renewable projects, with some projections favoring renewables due to faster permitting and expanded transmission. Rhodium Group models modest emissions reductions even if natural gas prices fall more than renewables, with larger cuts if renewables become much cheaper; the firm also expects natural gas pipelines to continue at roughly their current pace while renewable deployment accelerates. A key concern is that Republicans could exploit faster permitting for fossil fuels, though amendments attempt to limit presidential discrimination among energy sources—provisions some opponents say are too weak and others worry may be too strong.

Supporters include labor unions, clean and fossil energy companies, a few tribes, centrist policy organizations, and climate groups. Notably, Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich co-wrote the bill while opposing it did Green New Deal sponsors Ed Markey and Mazie Hirono; Al Gore and Genevieve Guenther oppose it, while Zeke Hausfather and David Pomerantz support it. The split has divided Democrats and the climate movement: some opponents favor permitting reform but want to wait until January for majorities in both houses to add stronger protections.

Legislatively, BAAJA is likely to pass the Republican-controlled Senate—where nearly every Republican and half of Democrats have advanced it—and could leave that chamber before Thanksgiving if amendments don't derail it. Its future in the House is more uncertain: crafted with limited input from members there, some Republicans including Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie express concern over transmission provisions, rural lawmakers may resist ceding local influence, and House Democrats such as Hakeem Jeffries have voiced concerns that could allow a coalition to defeat it. Trump supports permitting reform; if the bill isn't signed before year's end, it dies and would require starting over next session.
items.title: Congress’ energy permitting bill and what it means for communities, costs, and climate

As of November 18, Wall Street is preparing for the initial public offering (IPO) of Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, which is expected to launch on Thursday. Despite recent steep losses among hyperscalers and other stocks tied to the AI trade, anticipation from wealthy investors and retail buyers has been building ahead of what could be a record-setting debut. The IPO is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion (1,400,000,000,000 dollars), though it faces comparison with the SpaceX launch earlier this year that generated similar excitement and events.

Will Rhind, founder of GraniteShares in New York, plans to launch a 2x bull Anthropic exchange-traded fund (ETF) alongside a 2x bear product next week. He noted that judging by the number of people interacting with him about the offering, this could be even bigger than SpaceX.

According to industry estimates based on regulatory filings, the market was preparing for at least 11 leveraged single-stock ETFs from seven issuers in coming days, with retail investors accounting for much of the interest. One advertisement posted on StockTwits read: "Artificial intelligence meets human conviction with the 2X Long Anthropic Daily ETF from Tradr. Coming soon!"

Vanda Research said it expects Anthropic itself to attract about $250 million (250,000,000 dollars) in net retail buying, based on its analysis of activity on listing days and the volume of pre-IPO perpetual futures traded on Hyperliquid. Such a level would double the record $118 million (118,000,000 dollars) of retail buying for the SpaceX IPO.

Karl Cheong, head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners in Toronto, pointed to the selloff in bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a sign that retail investors want to raise cash to buy Anthropic. He described it as "the first frontier model that retail investors can access easily on a public market." Ninepoint plans to launch an ETF for Canadian investors combining leveraged exposure to Anthropic with a covered call strategy generating income.

Banks have also planned select events, including product launches tied to the stock, client livestreams, and merchandise. Goldman Sachs organized a launch event on Tuesday attended by its president John Waldron as well as Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and co-founder and president Daniela Amodei. JPMorgan plans to livestream the IPO for clients and has prepared merchandise such as t-shirts and laptop covers; Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei and his team were at the bank's offices all day on Friday meeting investors. Anthropic declined to comment on these events.

Not everyone is jumping on the bandwagon, however. London-based Ben Preston of Orbis Global Equity Strategy, a long-only stock-picking fund with a retail investor base, said the fund will not be buying Anthropic at the IPO. He called it "a very expensive valuation to pay for a company which is unproven" if it comes in at an IPO value around $1.5 trillion.

Although StockTwits users gave the anticipated IPO an "extremely bullish" score of 85 out of 100 based on its site poll, 67 per cent of more than 18,000 members who responded said they did not plan to buy Anthropic during the initial offering. Only 20 per cent said they will buy, while another 13 per cent said they would wait to see the price.

SpaceX has since had a mixed record: shares priced at $135 in the IPO jumped to $150 then briefly as high as $225 before dropping as low as $104. They now trade around $142.

Mitchell Caplan, chairman and CEO of Willow Wealth and former CEO of E-Trade Financial, said that as Anthropic's launch date approached, he had seen the excitement grow over getting a piece of whatever is allocated to retail.

Interest has also been building abroad, with many British platforms inviting retail investors to send orders for shares. Jordan Sinclair, president of Robinhood UK, noted that historically retail investors have stayed on the sidelines when it comes to public listings. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, a British platform serving high-net-worth investors, said the IPO highlights the divide between connected buyers who can get in pre-IPO and retail investors who end up pleading with brokers for part of an allocation.

She compared this dynamic to arriving at a glamorous launch party: institutional backers on the VIP guest list gain early entry behind closed doors, while latecomers are left paying a steep entry fee after the best festivities have already occurred.
items.title: Wall Street Prepares for Anthropic IPO Frenzy Amid Broader AI Stock Slump

items.summary: Apple's iPhone software has accumulated many features over the years, with newer capabilities—particularly those relying on Siri AI—easy to miss unless users regularly explore Settings or keep up with updates. The article outlines fifteen such functions across camera, photo editing, sharing, Safari, Lock Screen, Home Screen, and system appearance settings. In Camera, swiping to Siri mode or long-pressing the Camera Control lets users point at an object and ask questions; pointing food can trigger Look Up Nutrition, and event flyers can be added directly to a calendar by saying “Add this to my calendar.” These capabilities require Apple Intelligence and Siri AI and are available only on compatible iPhones in supported languages and regions. In Photos, pausing a video lets users select Save Video Frame as Photo from the three-dot menu; the resulting still retains original date, time, and location metadata. The Captured by Me collection separates screenshots and downloaded images, while an Identity Documents section helps locate IDs and passports. Users can enable Show Ratings Control to rate photos one to five stars for library filtering. Albums can be turned into videos via Start Slideshow with customizable transitions and music. Apple's Clean Up tool removes objects from a photo using on-device Fast processing or High Quality Private Cloud Compute, while the Extend tool expands image borders through Edit > Tools > Extend or the Crop tool. Spatial Reframe under Edit > Tools > Reframe adjusts apparent camera viewpoint after capture. iCloud Shared Albums now share photos and videos in full resolution rather than reducing quality. Safari's Notify Me option monitors websites for changes such as products returning to stock, with presets like Back in Stock or custom descriptions of what to track and how often. The Lock Screen clock can switch to a compact layout via Customise, positioning it closer to the date; Home Screen widgets can be resized by dragging a corner or selecting a larger gallery option. Liquid Glass appearance is adjustable under Settings > Appearance between clearer and more tinted versions. Alarm volume can be kept independent of ringtone volume by turning off Match Ringtone Volume in Sounds & Haptics > Alarms and Timers. Apple states most everyday customization and Photos features are supported on iPhone 11 and later, while Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features require iPhone 15 Pro and later, with availability also depending on language and region.
items.title: 15 lesser-known iPhone features in iOS 27 and later

items.summary: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress confirmed that the company's board has decided not to reinstate founder and former CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down on November 11 following reports about his personal conduct. Huang had led the AI chipmaker for 33 years before resigning as president, CEO, and board member, having earlier expressed willingness to return if directors believed it would benefit the company. Kress stated that 'the board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen,' and Nvidia has begun considering both internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. Despite this leadership transition, Nvidia raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to 75%, up from an earlier projection of 70%. The stronger outlook follows the company's latest quarterly results and continued demand for AI computing infrastructure. Kress said the company would remain focused on customers, employees, and shareholders, expressing confidence in long-tenured staff who built the business. She also dismissed suggestions that Nvidia could lose its biggest customers without Huang, noting that demand for its computing platforms remains strong and customers continue seeking additional supply. The central question now is whether Nvidia can preserve these relationships under a new permanent leader while navigating the succession challenge of replacing one of technology's most influential founders.
items.title: Nvidia Board Rejects Jensen Huang's Return as CEO; Company Raises Growth Forecast to 75%

items.summary: Armed conflict is at its highest level since records began: the Uppsala Conflict Data Program recorded 61 active state-based conflicts in 2024 and 65 in 2025, the most since 1946 and roughly double the figure a decade earlier. Almost all are civil wars between governments and armed groups, with a growing share drawing in outside states (date-49-53). These conflicts fall disproportionately on poor countries: OECD estimates that 72% of people living on less than $2.15 a day reside in fragile countries, many affected by conflict, including among the 18 classed as extremely fragile such as Afghanistan, Sudan, and Congo (quantity-59-62). Research has not kept pace; Dube identifies three obstacles—conflict and income are jointly determined so correlations reveal little about causation, fieldwork is dangerous and expensive, and data collection itself breaks down where statistical systems stop working and official surveys end (Dube)—while Callen notes that less than 1% of studies in the American Economic Association’s registry of randomised controlled trials come from the 18 most fragile countries (quantity-132-134). Higher income can push conflict in opposite directions. The opportunity cost channel applies Gary Becker’s economic model of crime to rebellion: fighting is like a job, so rising wages make recruits more expensive and armed groups shrink (entity-2824-2837). The rapacity channel works the other way—conflict as violent theft means richer states or those with valuable resources become bigger prizes. To separate them, Dube and Juan Vargas studied two Colombian commodities: coffee on small labour-intensive farms where price changes mainly affect wages, versus oil extracted capital-intensively where price rises mainly increase what can be appropriated (entity-3456-3467). When coffee prices collapsed, attacks rose more in coffee-growing municipalities; when oil prices rose, attacks increased in oil-producing areas. The mechanisms lined up—coffee shocks moved wages while oil shocks raised royalties and kidnappings of politicians as revenue was siphoned off. The pattern holds beyond Colombia: Berman and Couttenier divided sub-Saharan Africa into 50-by-50-kilometre grid cells and found falling agricultural prices increase conflict in cells growing more of those crops, while Berman, Couttenier, Rohner, and Thoenig found rising mineral prices intensify fighting near mines (quantity-4214-4216). A meta-analysis of 46 natural experiments by Blair, Christensen, and Rudkin confirmed agricultural prices reduce conflict while oil, gas, and artisanal mineral prices increase it (quantity-4484-4494). Progress also came from shrinking the unit of analysis—from country-year to municipality-year to grid-cell-year—with satellite and mobile phone data processed with AI tools opening new questions. Hannes Mueller and co-authors trained a neural network to detect destroyed buildings in satellite images of Syrian cities, radar satellites measure damage in Gaza through cloud and smoke (entity-4670-4679), and Dube used anonymised Afghanistan phone records—call volumes falling during the evening prayer window—to measure religious adherence. Building state capacity during war: Callen describes a reform with Afghanistan’s Ministry of Education to tackle administrative failures, where 41% of teachers were absent, only about 30% found had government documents, and 60% reported late salaries delayed around three and a half months (quantity-5802-5895). The reform used biometric registration and mobile money to pay roughly 30,000 employees across three provinces in a randomised controlled trial. Callen cautions technology is no panacea—the human element remains—while signing up was costly for teachers short-term with benefits arriving only over time (quantity-6104-6120). Empirically the strongest predictor of success was whether teachers’ communities believed the government would defeat the Taliban; that doubt proved well founded, as the system shut down after the takeover. Rebel governance and inclusive democracy: Callen contrasts Afghanistan’s externally imposed institutions leaving the Taliban no political voice except violence with Nepal, where Maoist rebels ran schools, courts, and mobilisation around Janajati rights during war (entity-7144-8069). The peace agreement created a decentralised federal democracy suited to ethnic diversity. Callen finds Janajati citizens are now more knowledgeable about the post-war constitution and engaged in politics; candidate-selecting elites come increasingly from historically excluded groups—leaders trained in the Maoists’ civilian arm—and rival parties have become more inclusive (entity-7325-8069). Development must take conflict seriously: military and development spending in Afghanistan reached $3 trillion, more than the Marshall Plan, with 170,000 people killed before Taliban rule returned. As poverty falls in peaceful countries, extreme poor concentrate in conflict-affected places—“draining the swamp” leaves its thorniest bits (quantity-8007-8069). Dube calls for more evidence on interventions in fragile states and tracking natural resource royalties.
items.title: What drives civil war in poor countries?

items.summary: Labour's North Northumberland MP David Smith has urged Northumberland County Council to accelerate the processing of heating oil support payments as global conflicts drive energy prices higher. Approximately 23,000 homes in Northumberland rely on oil systems because they are not connected to the mains gas supply. Unlike gas, which is protected by the Ofgem Energy Price Cap, oil tank-filling costs have risen sharply for households. A freedom of information request from 21 September showed that just over a third of applicants had received funding: Smith reported 328 applications with only 112 approved and total payments amounting to £36,123. The Conservative-led council responded by citing more recent figures showing significantly higher approval rates almost two months later, stating that more than 160 applicants and 40 venues had been supported and that there was no backlog for residents seeking assistance. A spokesperson explained that those not receiving support are applicants who have failed to demonstrate their household is vulnerable or struggling due to low income. The government provided £5m to the county council through its Crisis and Resilience fund in April, including almost £500,000 earmarked for households facing heating oil costs. Bamburgh Conservative councillor Guy Renner-Thompson, who has a home using a heating oil system, called on the government for additional financial support, noting that the council fully expected to spend the entire £498,459 heating oil allocation.
items.title: Northumberland MP urges council to speed up heating oil support payments amid soaring energy prices
