Energy bills for the typical Great Britain household are projected to reach £2,166 a year from January, according to Cornwall Insight. The leading forecaster attributes this rise partly to pressure on gas and electricity prices stemming from the Middle East conflict. Its forecast indicates that the government's cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to increase by 26%, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, representing one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record. This prediction arrives as Ofgem prepares next Wednesday to set new energy rates for January through March via a fresh energy price cap.

The forecast stands well above Cornwall's late September projection that the cap would rise by 16% to £1,999 a year following an October increase in gas market prices. That earlier estimate had been driven by escalating violence in the Middle East and deepening fears over Europe's gas storage levels. Craig Lowrey, retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, noted that energy bills were already climbing in October before rising again into the new year, with colder January weather pushing up consumption while households grapple with the cost of living crisis.

The price rise comes as a setback for the government after chancellor John Healey pledged to set 'a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe' in his maiden budget last month. To cushion struggling households this winter, Healey promised a one-off £100 payment in January reaching 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.

The household energy payment totals about £2.6bn and will be delivered directly into bank accounts alongside the warm home discount, which offers roughly six million means-tested households across England, Wales and Scotland a £150 reduction on winter fuel bills. The measures follow electricity levy cuts over the past year that reduced costs by around £150 annually, plus a Treasury commitment to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity for 29 million households until July, extending annual savings of about £50.

The forecast coincides with Office for National Statistics figures showing headline inflation rose to 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, driven by higher petrol prices and a record-high diesel price.
items.title: GB energy price cap forecast to jump 26% as Middle East conflict drives up bills

items.summary: Andy Burnham said he would consider cutting national insurance for young people 'very carefully', but declined a firm commitment, noting that any change is a matter for the budget and must be weighed against affordability. He described reviewing all available evidence rather than ruling on policy outright. A Tuesday report by former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn proposed gradually lowering NICs paid by firms for under-25s, starting with retail and hospitality companies, and doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. Burnham defended his predecessor Keir Starmer and former chancellor Rachel Reeves against claims that their welfare reforms were wrong, arguing his approach is 'a very different proposition' focused on supporting young people rather than the crude cuts pursued by Conservatives and Reform. He cited the Youth Guarantee as an example of employer support for taking on young people, while also acknowledging existing exemptions: no employer NICs are paid for workers younger than 21 or apprentices under 25 unless they earn above £50,270, and employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000 for non-apprentices aged 21-24. Official figures show nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, which Burnham framed as evidence that a fundamentally different, more localised approach is needed rather than a top-down tick-box system.
items.title: Burnham weighing NIC cuts to boost youth employment amid welfare reform debate

items.summary: The States of Deliberation is set to decide next week whether to temporarily reduce 2027 social insurance contributions by 0.5%, lowering employee (primary Class 1) rates to 7.1% and self-employed (Class 2) rates to 12.1%. The proposal would apply to both employees and the self-employed, according to Forward Guernsey deputies Gavin St Pier and Tom Rylatt, who intend to bring an amendment to the Social Insurance (Rates of Contributions and Benefits etc.) Ordinance, 2026. St Pier cited global events, including the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars, as having created significant economic pressures across the community on Guernsey. He noted that contributions have risen each year under a 10-year programme of increases; without this amendment, employee contributions would have increased by 1% since 2021 and self-employed contributions by 1.6%. Rylatt said the cut would give working islanders "breathing room," arguing that with little sign of cost-of-living pressures easing in 2027 and tax reform now decided, this year is a suitable time to use the flexibility built into the Employment and Social Security (ESS) 10-year plan. He estimated the amendment for 2027 would amount to a loss of between £8m and £9m for the Guernsey Insurance Fund, but described it as "a one-off departure from the existing trajectory." The article reports no vote outcome or further detail beyond this proposal.
items.title: Guernsey States to debate a cut in 2027 social security contributions

items.summary: Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as the seventh actor to play James Bond, a role he described as “the honour of a lifetime” and “a dream come true.” Amazon boss Jeff Bezos said at an event in California that he was “heavily involved” in the casting. He explained that his team were initially biased against Pattinson because he is already famous, preferring someone more unknown, but added: “But in the screening test, it’s so obvious. He is James Bond.” The final five actors selected for the next 007 were described as “extraordinarily talented,” though Bezos said there was “something special about Rob.” Pattinson's debut will be the first Bond film released since Amazon's acquisition of MGM. Reactions have been broadly positive, if mixed. The royal family posted on Instagram: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond”, while a spokesperson for UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is “obviously delighted” and called the role an “amazing opportunity.” Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump's health secretary, shared an AI-generated image of himself as 007 with a gun replaced by a giant carrot and captioned it: “Food. Real Food,” drawing mockery online. Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve told GQ that the most important quality he sought was belief that Pattinson is a killer, since “more than a spy, Bond is an assassin.” He also wanted unapologetic panache, strong charisma, sensuality, dark humor, physical strength and deep intelligence in the eyes. Villeneuve previously worked with Pattinson on Dune: Part Three. Co-stars Rami Malek called him “extraordinary,” Ralph Fiennes said he was still in love with Daniel Craig but believed Pattinson is a great actor who will be great, Elizabeth Debicki said she thought he would be “the perfect Bond” and described him as beautiful, funny and smart, and Brad Pitt backed the casting while joking about playing a future villain. George Lazenby, the 87-year-old oldest living 007 actor from 1969's On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, welcomed Pattinson to “the most exclusive club in the world.” Pattinson follows six previous Bonds: Sean Connery, Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. Production on Bond 26 is expected to start next year, but filming will be delayed until Pattinson completes The Batman Part II, with Steven Soderbergh helping shoot the final weeks after Matt Reeves faced a personal issue. This means the earliest release could be in the second half of 2028 — seven years since No Time To Die and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.
items.title: Reactions to Robert Pattinson's Casting as James Bond

items.summary: An update released by Apple on Tuesday triggered a major outage affecting many of its online services, including full outages of Apple Music, the App Store, and AppleCare, along with issues in the iCloud sign-in interface. Downdetector.com also recorded a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay. In an emailed statement, Apple said that 'Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,' noting it was working to bring remaining systems online; its status page later indicated no services were down. The incident followed other major technology breakdowns across the week. On Monday, United Airlines experienced a system outage lasting more than 90 minutes that forced flight delays, and earlier in the same period an FAA network malfunction prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers. That day banks were also affected after thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major US banks and through Zelle following a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase; Chase said Monday the problems were not caused by a cyberattack and confirmed Tuesday its systems were operating normally. Marriott International, the largest US hotel operator, also had technology issues affecting sign-in on Marriott.com and the Bonvoy app, though a company review found no indication it was cybersecurity-related. Earlier in the week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and workplace tools including Outlook, Teams, and AI assistant Copilot; Microsoft stated there was 'no indication' that malicious activity or artificial intelligence agents caused the disruptions. Across these incidents, multiple companies reported no sign of cyberattacks as the cause.
items.title: Apple Outage Amid String of Major Tech Breakdowns

items.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce announced on Tuesday that China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years. Under the extension, Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with applicable laws and regulations. A ministry spokesperson attributed the agreement to consensus reached between the leaders of both countries, noting that multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations were conducted in a spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation. The two sides also reportedly reached positive consensus on additional issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment. Both parties said they will expedite their respective domestic procedures to implement the agreed measures as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation. The spokesperson added that both countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences, and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral relations. The preliminary joint arrangement was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products. The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries. No specific dates for the two-year extension or implementation timeline were provided beyond the reference to Carney's January visit when the original arrangement was reached.
items.title: China-Canada Extend Trade Exemptions for Two Years

items.summary: The article opens by noting that China and Korea share a relationship spanning thousands of years, with the narrow Yellow Sea today hosting some of the world's busiest ports. It frames this trade activity as being driven largely by a generation of young people on both sides who possess language skills and cultural understanding, promoting greater mutual comprehension and forging new connections. For many of these individuals, their appreciation for the other culture originated during university years and continues to influence career choices and future plans. The piece presents this generational dynamic as an engine behind deepening bilateral ties across the sea, though it offers no specific figures, named actors, or concrete examples beyond this characterization. No quantitative data on trade volumes, port statistics, or individual profiles are provided in the text available for synthesis, so any deeper analysis of causal mechanisms remains unstated rather than reported here. The framing is explicitly presented as an editorial feature (marked by untrusted source text), and its claims about what drives cross-sea trade rest entirely on this narrative assertion without supporting metrics within the excerpted material. As such, the summary reflects only the qualitative relationship described: a long historical bond expressed through contemporary young professionals whose cultural fluency is positioned as central to ongoing economic engagement across the Yellow Sea's busy ports. The document does not quantify these drivers or attribute specific trade flows to them; it simply situates human and cultural exchange within an established pattern of commercial activity between the two nations' coastal hubs.
items.title: Assignment Asia: What's Driving Trade Across the Yellow Sea

items.summary: The article reports that 80% of the world's stomach cancer cases occur in Asia, framing this concentration as a significant regional health challenge. In response to these high rates, scientists in Singapore are investigating changes in DNA and RNA to detect early-stage signals of cancer, with the goal of improving patient survival chances. The piece notes that artificial intelligence is assisting researchers by accelerating their work on identifying these biological markers. No specific figures beyond the 80% statistic are provided, nor are details given about particular AI methods, research institutions, or clinical outcomes.
items.title: Asia's Stomach Cancer Burden and Singapore's AI-Driven Research

items.summary:
In a speech to the National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC), Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood pledged to confront what she called the "corrosive and growing perception" of so-called two-tier policing, without asserting that such bias actually exists. She acknowledged that most officers police impartially but noted there have been examples of differential treatment that motivated actors have exploited to fuel the idea. The article frames this as part of Mahmood's strategy of disarming critics by partly agreeing with them while remaining a Labour cabinet minister.

On evidence, a Guardian-referenced report found that Black people remained more likely than any other ethnic group to be subjected to nearly every form of force, from handcuffing and dog bites to firearms and Tasers, when compared with population or arrest figures. A More in Common poll earlier this year found a third of Britons believe police treat minority-ethnic backgrounds more favourably than white people, marking a doubling over the previous two years.

Mahmood's proposed measures include developing a new "impartiality standard" to consolidate guidance on impartiality principles and build confidence that everyone is treated equally regardless of race, faith or other characteristics. She also plans to fast-track talented recruits from outside policing into senior ranks to address what she described as sometimes inadequate leadership.

She will warn officers against engaging with activist groups and tell them to "leave the politics to the politicians," cautioning against "misguided attempts at course correction" where pursuing equality leads instead to differential treatment. She also lamented that, 33 years after the murder of Black teenager Stephen Lawrence, the proportion of Black officers remains virtually unchanged.

The article notes Mahmood's criticism targets the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, which states that producing equality of policing outcomes does not mean treating everyone 'the same', a position frequently criticised by Conservatives and Reform UK. The piece also satirised the two-tier concept via Robert Hutton from The Critic during the 2024 summer riots.

Other agenda items include Chris Bryant giving evidence to the Commons Northern Ireland committee at 9.30am, Yvette Cooper speaking at the King's Fund conference at 11am, Andy Burnham facing Kemi Badenoch at PMQs at noon, and MPs beginning a debate on an opposition day motion opposing most features of the Prime Minister's proposed UK-EU reset deal after 12.30pm.
items.title: Mahmood to tackle 'perception' of two-tier policing in NPCC speech

items.summary: Jassim al-Asadi, a 69-year-old Iraqi environmentalist born in Iraq's central marshes, has returned to the wetlands three years after being kidnapped, tortured for two weeks, and accused of running an Israeli spy network. In February 2023, gunmen cut off his car on the road south as he drove from Baghdad toward his hometown of Chibayish after a meeting with the Iraqi president about aid for destitute marsh families. He was blindfolded, beaten, and driven to what he believed was farmland, where captors showed him a screen displaying global networks connecting countries 'to Tel Aviv' and accused him of leading such a network from world capitals while ferrying journalists into Iran. After refusing to confess despite beatings, they placed a plastic bag over his head until he nearly suffocated, plunged his head underwater repeatedly, ran electric shocks through his body starting at the feet moving up to genitals, chest and nose, and suspended him from the ceiling beating his arms with metal chains while demanding 'Sign a confession or write your will.' Given an hour to either confess or write a will under threat of immediate death, Asadi wrote that he loved Iraq, had done nothing wrong, wished for national independence and strength, opposed all hatred and division, asked his wife not to be too upset, and wished his children would follow in his footsteps even if 'that path led to my death.' During the two weeks held captive, he recited poetry—particularly Saadi Youssef's poem In Those Days—to distract himself from fear. Instead of killing him, captors threw him onto a vehicle floor and left him by a Baghdad road near where family waited; injured and weak, he insisted on returning home to Chibayish the next day, where hundreds of marsh residents welcomed him with flags and posters. Asadi says he knows the militia that kidnapped him and believes the government did as well because his cousin's driver had memorized the license plate number. The Iraqi government pledged release but Iran-backed militias in some areas have grown more powerful than security forces, so it was ultimately Asadi's Bani Asad tribe that won his freedom by mobilizing 400 armed clan members to surround a kidnapper's house and threaten death if he died; Alwash said 'Jassim was known — everybody was like, why mess around with Jassim.' As part of the release deal, Asadi did not pursue the case in court. He says it never occurred to him he faced danger because Nature Iraq is purely environmental and unaffiliated with any political party. After being freed, he refused asylum offers in Europe as his captors wanted him gone, instead requesting asylum for two children now living in Sweden so they would be safe while he continued working the marshes; a third child lives in the United States. His co-founder Azzam Alwash said intelligence services of three different countries told him after Asadi's seizure that he too was at risk and has not returned to Iraq since. Iran, according to Alwash, operates on an 'operating theory' that Nature Iraq is a Mossad operation it cannot understand why Western governments would fund the environment; those suspicions date to 2016 when the group began working with Iranian conservationists on the Persian Leopard in mountains between Iran and Iraq, after which Iran arrested nine related Iranian conservationists accusing them of espionage—the Iranian-Canadian co-founder of the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation died in detention while others spent years imprisoned. Nature Iraq has raised a generation of environmentalists mainly from southern Iraq and Kurdistan, built floating islands for water buffalo breeders and reed guest houses for tourists, lobbied governments on water policies reviving the marshes—primarily against Turkey's dams reducing downstream flow—and constructed natural cleaning ponds to remove sewage toxins since there is no treatment plant; at its peak it had 94 staff operating in Iraq and Kurdistan. In 2018 secret allegations of public fund misuse led Iraqi prosecutors to freeze bank accounts, dropping the investigation four years later for lack of evidence, leaving only four paid-staff-able members. Asadi's arrest and Iran's imprisonment of Iranian environmentalists have chilled activism; volunteer Muntadher Abedali, 21, said after the kidnapping people asked 'why are you working with Jassim? It's dangerous,' yet he taught himself English to contribute stories to Climate Stories as a voice for impoverished marsh residents lacking political power. The marshes themselves suffered five years of devastating drought that dried some wetlands and left remaining water brackish, stunting reeds while buffalo died from lack of food and contaminated water; herders fled with their animals seeking water or city outskirts but are now returning to repopulate tiny floating islands where residents live a way little changed since Sumerian times over 4,000 years ago. With winter rains after the drought, water levels have risen more than one third, though fishermen report few and small fish; Raad, 23, lost seven buffalo that sickened or died plus sold others during constant moves every two to three months, dropping from a herd of 50 to fewer than 20 but now getting up to four quarts of milk daily per animal. Alwash noted the flood cycle fostering biodiversity ended in 2019 when Turkey's Elisu dam project began capturing downstream water; Asadi concluded his ordeal showed 'this isn't an easy path — it requires sacrifices and strength,' urging people to work hard for their country, nature, and environment.
items.title: Iraqi environmentalist survives kidnapping by Iran-backed militia and returns to marshes

items.summary: As more than 200 countries gather in Turkey for COP31 climate talks, greenhouse gas emissions from the two largest polluters—China and the United States—are diverging. For roughly two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling after previously growing with increased coal use; Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, calls this 'a remarkable change.' The reductions come from expanding renewable energy and batteries that displace coal, plus electric vehicles cutting oil demand. Myllyvirta says these are larger cuts than expected: his group found China's emissions dropped 3% in the most recent quarter, its largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic. Alex Wang, a UCLA Law professor specializing in Chinese climate policy, notes that if the U.S. deployed large-scale renewables and batteries like China, it could cut more; instead, U.S. emissions rose in 2025 as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating—making the U.S. 'the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year,' per a recent United Nations scientists report. Emissions are projected to fall slightly this year with less coal, but Wang warns they could drop further if clean-energy deployment scaled up; he attributes the shortfall to policy whiplash from shifting administrations: Biden expanded funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles, while Trump cut that funding and added regulatory hurdles. Wang says China began building its emissions-reducing infrastructure about twenty years ago amid record city air pollution, using consistent five-year plans to develop supply chains for solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and EVs into a global leadership position; Myllyvirta adds the power sector is falling as coal use declines while solar, wind and nuclear rise—even though China has built many new coal plants that often run only as backup. In transportation, two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales are now electric vehicles per recent data from the China Passenger Car Association. Wang also cautions that China's emissions remain outsized relative to the rest of the world; meanwhile its clean-tech exports—solar, batteries and EVs—to countries like Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines help reduce their fossil-fuel dependence. Kingsmill Bond of Ember says these exports have only grown since 'the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran,' a phrase attributed directly to him in the article rather than as an established fact. At COP31, which will emphasize electrification commitments, Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, expects China to promote its clean-tech trade and says its dominant position 'will not go away' but may be further consolidated, leaving the U.S. struggling; he frames this as a competitive challenge rather than an environmental one. The White House responded to last year's emissions rise by citing President Trump's 'energy dominance agenda,' with spokesperson Taylor Rodgers telling NPR that affordable energy sources are being unleashed and many nations rely on U.S. oil and gas supply.
items.title: China and the U.S. remain top emitters, but only China is reducing them

items.summary: Concerns are mounting that the United States could sanction judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), including Navi Pillay—the ad hoc judge appointed by The Gambia and this year's Nobel peace prize winner—if the court rules Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. This would be the first time the ICJ has found a state responsible for committing genocide, raising questions about how to prove intent in a crime defined as acts carried out with the 'intent to destroy, in whole or in part' a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors argue that patterns of conduct by Myanmar's military—including killing people as they fled—demonstrate deliberate attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017. Judges have reportedly sought advice on protecting their assets from potential US sanctions, since a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the legal threshold for the crime. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a thinktank close to the White House, has predicted that such a ruling would prompt the US to sanction the ICJ. Both the US and Israel fear the judgment may clarify how intent is established, setting precedent that could later be used against Israel in Gaza over its conduct there. Myanmar denies committing genocide, claiming its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents rather than an ethnic group. The article notes that the ICJ settles interstate disputes, distinguishing it from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes. The US has already imposed sanctions on ICC judges after arrest warrants were issued against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and announced sanctions against the entire ICC as a 'rogue court,' fearing it could target US troops. Pillay is required to act as an independent jurist rather than advocate for The Gambia. Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, warned both Pillay and all 15 ICJ judges that Washington 'will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops,' asserting last month that Pillay is attempting to lower the standard for proving genocide so it could later be applied against American and allied soldiers. In remarks addressed to Pillay, Waltz said his administration would watch how the ICJ handles these proceedings 'very closely.' US secretary of state Marco Rubio stated in a speech on Friday that international law has been used by some as an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles, warning the ICC against quoting laws to 'men with swords.' Israel has previously criticized adverse advisory opinions from the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring it to admit more aid into Gaza and cooperate with UNRWA. A 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states argued that in judging intent, the ICJ should examine a range of 'facts and circumstances' assessed 'comprehensively and holistically,' stressing that genocide is not defined solely by killings but also includes treatment of children, gender-based violence, and forced displacement. The US had previously taken a more benign view of the Hague-based court under Antony Blinken as secretary of state, who determined that Myanmar had committed genocide. ICJ judges serve nine-year terms elected by both the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly. Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before imposing sanctions. On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan; although evidence would be hard to obtain, this may increase US willingness to abandon its plan to sanction the ICC.
items.title: Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling

items.summary: The Ghanaian government has defended its decision to buy a new presidential aircraft after the purchase drew widespread criticism over its price, as many citizens continue struggling with high living costs. The French-made Dassault Aviation Falcon 6X was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m (£46m), though it is frequently described in headlines and elsewhere as costing around $60m. Parliament approved the purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise military aviation, which also includes four Airbus helicopters. The government argues that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and needed to replace an ageing Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems including corrosion and fuel-tank leakages, and was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs. Officials say the new jet offers a longer flying range that reduces refuelling stops on international trips. The controversy intensified because President John Mahama's administration sought to demonstrate economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance; notably, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet while in opposition, prompting questions about why his government proceeded with the purchase. Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the timing and priorities, arguing the expenditure fell during high cost-of-living pressures and alarmingly high youth unemployment, accusing the governing National Democratic Congress of hypocrisy after its senior figures had strongly opposed such a plane when out of power; he also called for greater transparency over how the aircraft was financed. On social media, some users argued the money could have been spent on more pressing needs, with one X user posting that it 'could employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers.' Parliament's defence committee chairman Peter Lanchene Toobu said his party never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle but objected to the timing during severe economic difficulties while Ghana sought a $3bn IMF bailout; he argued that improved macroeconomic stability and cheaper imports now justify the purchase. Ofosu added that the government bought the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and better conditions. Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu dismissed claims of misplaced priorities, pointing to falling construction-material prices and lower borrowing costs as evidence of economic improvement; he cited cement costing 115 cedis (£7.5) per bag in 2024 versus 80 cedis today. The dispute also extended to the aircraft's interior after claims it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom, which Ofosu denied, saying there is no bathroom because President Mahama 'has no intention of bathing in the air,' though he acknowledged reclining seats that convert into sleeping arrangements but rejected a dedicated bedroom. Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin of the University of Ghana said presidential safety was paramount but argued the timing remained difficult to justify amid austerity, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges, calling for a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying rather than leasing the jet better serves national interests.
items.title: Ghana's $60m presidential jet purchase draws public and political backlash amid cost-of-living concerns

items.summary: Lucio Usobiaga of Mexico won the 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize, also called the 'Nobel Prize of Gastronomy,' for his project Arca Tierra. The prize was created in 2016 by the government of Spain's Basque autonomous region and the Basque Culinary Center, and awards 100,000 euros (about $110,000) to a winner-chosen project. Usobiaga said he wants people to know that chinampero farmers have lived in the chinampas for millennia and that their work has mostly gone unseen. Arca Tierra is described as a network of farmers and Mexico's culinary community helping preserve Xochimilco, an ancient pre-Aztec system of agricultural canal islands built into wetlands in the southern valley of Mexico City. The project cultivates 6 hectares (about 15 acres) within the chinampas and works with 50 farming families across Xochimilco, Puebla, Hidalgo, and the state of Mexico; these farms supply around 60 restaurants in Mexico City with fresh produce. Usobiaga told Food & Wine that the chinampa soil's high organic matter from lake sediments gives food grown there a special flavor, adding: 'I can tell, like from the first bite, when I'm eating a beet from the chinampas.' He cited buying products grown by chinamperos, visiting the chinampas, and paying farmers for ecosystem services as ways to support the system. Usobiaga said he also wants to attract more young people to continue farming there, noting that international recognition is helping encourage interest. The chinampas are described as the last remaining habitat for wild axolotls (Ambystoma mexicanum). Usobiaga explained their premise that 'the chinampero farmer is the guardian and custodian of the chinampas,' including its canals and animals, pointing to biofilters developed to exclude predators and clean water so axolotls can live there. He added that traditional farming and agroecology avoid toxic chemicals and help restore ecosystemic services. The article notes the chinampas filter water back to the aquifer, sequester carbon, hold biodiversity, and sustain culture; Usobiaga warned they are being lost to urbanization and abandonment while chinampero resistance remains strong but needs support in many ways. Mongabay's Aimee Gabay reported on these farmers in 2024. The banner image of Lucio Usobiaga is courtesy of Pablo Antoli.
items.title: Lucio Usobiaga Wins 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize for Protecting Mexico's Chinampas

items.summary:
A new report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) finds that wildlife trafficking persists in West and Central Africa despite increased enforcement, with Nigeria remaining a central export hub for elephant ivory and pangolin scales shipped to Asia. Although enforcement operations have grown since 2020—resulting in more incidents detected, arrests, and prosecutions—the illegal trade has barely been disrupted. Traffickers relocated their operations from Lagos's Lekki Craft Market, where law enforcement presence increased, to smaller port cities with weaker oversight such as Enungu (about 230 kilometers/140 miles inland) and Port Harcourt. Criminal networks have also adapted by concealing contraband in legitimate products like edible moringa seeds and channeling illicit funds through bank transfers and underground banking systems.

The report's findings underscore the gap between enforcement activity and actual disruption: of 58 documented wildlife crime incidents in Nigeria since January 2021, only six resulted in prosecutions. Across West and Central Africa, the arrest-to-conviction rate stands at just 16%, with low-level actors such as poachers and middlemen typically taking the fall while powerful kingpins and corrupt officials avoid justice. EIA's Justin Gosling noted that Nigeria had achieved its first high-level wildlife trafficking prosecutions in years but cautioned that competing crime interests and broader economic issues limit progress.

The trade centers on pangolin scales, used in traditional Chinese medicine despite having no proven medicinal value, and elephant ivory—both highly coveted by Asian buyers. Pangolins are the world's most trafficked mammal; with Southeast Asian supplies depleted, poachers have increasingly targeted Africa, where two of four species are now endangered and two vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. All eight pangolin species received CITES protection in 2017 banning cross-border commercial sale.

By volume, Nigeria remained the region's primary exit point for illegal wildlife from 2021 to 2026, with more than 50,000 kg (more than 110,000 lb) of elephant ivory and pangolin scales seized. Gabon recorded the most wildlife crime incidents in that period, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo followed with more than 16,000 kg (about 35,000 lb) seized.

Experts warn against a 'leaking bucket' dynamic, where crackdowns simply displace trafficking to other regions. Ruth Musgrave of the Elephant Protection Initiative Foundation emphasized that enforcement agencies must prosecute the right people and disrupt networks rather than only targeting peripheral actors. Gosling stressed that preventing wildlife crime is especially critical because harm occurs at the outset—killing an animal or felling a tree—even if traffickers are later caught, leaving authorities with 'just stockrooms full of dead animals.' A glimmer of hope lies in Nigeria's forthcoming Endangered Species Conservation and Protection Bill 2024, though experts caution that such measures must be adopted and enforced across the entire region.
items.title: West and Central Africa Remain Hubs of Illegal Wildlife Trade Despite Enforcement Efforts

items.summary: Education First (EF) released its largest global ranking of adult English proficiency on Wednesday, with Japan placing 86th out of 123 countries. This represented an improvement of 10 places over the previous year, when Japan ranked 96th; that prior edition marked an all-time low and extended a downward trend in Japanese English proficiency across recent years. The 2026 index drew on test results from 2.3 million participants across 117 countries and regions. Alongside its rank improvement, Japan moved up one proficiency band this year, shifting from the lowest category, "very low," to the "low" band. Despite these gains, EF noted that Japan still trailed peers in Asia and elsewhere: it ranked 36 places below South Korea's 50th-place finish, scored 450 points versus a global average of 485 (35 points below), performed worse than European countries such as Sweden, Austria, and Denmark at the top of the rankings, and showed weaker results in speaking and writing relative to reading. EF also found regional variation within Japan, with learners in urban hubs like Yokohama, Tokyo, and Kyoto outperforming those in Hiroshima, Shizuoka, and Kochi. As across many countries covered by the index, younger Japanese adults lagged most sharply: 18- to 20-year-olds recorded the lowest scores of all age groups. EF attributed this decline partly to the COVID-19 pandemic's knock-on effects on a cohort that took online rather than in-person English classes between 2019 and 2022, an effect observed both in Japan and worldwide. In response, Masato Suzuki, business development manager for EF Japan, said raising proficiency among this generation would create a bottom-up effect as they enter the workforce; Nana Gronning Ito, EF country manager, advised against relying solely on digital learning and instead emphasized real-life communication and experiencing the joy of expression even when making mistakes. The summary reflects only what is reported in the article, including its framing that Japan's improvement does not erase continued lags behind peers.
items.title: Japan Ranks 86th in EF's 2026 Adult English Proficiency Index After Rising from a Record Low

items.summary: South Africa is preparing for a potentially difficult summer as the established El Niño phenomenon—defined in the article as the warming of Pacific Ocean surface temperatures that influences global weather and drives extreme events like floods, droughts, and heat waves—is expected to intensify into a very intense 'super El Niño' by late 2026, with effects continuing until early 2027. The World Meteorological Organization is cited as the source of this expectation. This super El Niño raises risks of increased drought, heat waves, water stress, pasture loss for livestock, reduced cereal yields, and forest fires in southern Africa. Researchers specializing in pastoral and crop production argue that planting dates matter significantly: their study conducted at Cedara in KwaZulu-Natal's Midlands region—characterized by deep red clay soil with hot, humid summers—showed that earlier planting (December and January) generally produced better results when forage radish was sown over a four-month period relying solely on rainfall without fertilizer. This approach reflected conditions of smallholder farmers with limited access to irrigation and fertilizers. The study found that radish planted in December produces substantially more tubers, while radish planted in January yields more leafy, higher-protein forage; mineral concentrations such as phosphorus, potassium, and zinc are also higher in leaves when planting is earlier. Higher forage nutritional value supports faster livestock growth and health, whereas farmers who cannot grow sufficient quality forage risk income losses when animals lack food. The article notes that the study was conducted over a limited period of two planting seasons within a small area of KwaZulu-Natal's Midlands, meaning results may not apply to other South African regions with different soil types, climates, and rainfall patterns, and additional trials are needed using different crops, sowing periods, and rainfall conditions. The researchers recommend that farmers plan for a range of dates rather than fixed ones, adjusting planting within a season to accommodate early or late rains, since planting too early or too late can expose young plants to drought or flooding; they also emphasize the need for agricultural advisors, weather services, and researchers to translate seasonal forecasts into practical sowing recommendations before decisions are made. The article states that even simple management decisions like timely planting help farmers use available rainfall more efficiently without purchasing expensive new equipment.
items.title: Planting Date Strategy for Forage Radish Under South African El Niño Conditions

items.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola has won the closely contested Alaska Senate race, marking a decisive victory for Democrats in the US upper house. The win delivered the party's 56th Senate seat and became its ninth pickup from Republicans this cycle, giving them control of Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency alongside their regained House majority. Calling Peltola two weeks after counting began reflected Alaska's logistical difficulty collecting ballots across its remote territory; with 99% counted she held slightly more than 50%, while incumbent Dan S Sullivan trailed on under 46%. In her victory statement, Peltola said the 'status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,' recalling rural Alaskans facing hardship and pledging to fight corporate greed and put Alaska first. The race was complicated by an alleged effort reported by the New York Times to recruit a political unknown named Daniel J Sullivan—sharing a name with incumbent Dan S Sullivan—to confuse voters; after legal challenges, state courts allowed him on the ballot while election officials distinguished them in materials. Peltola denied knowledge of any plot, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor announced investigations into her campaign. The Trump administration filed suit to block certification if incumbent Sullivan lost, but a federal judge dismissed it following challenges from Alaska election officials, the Peltola campaign, and voting groups. Because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, confused voters could rank each Dan Sullivan first and second; after the non-incumbent candidate was eliminated, his votes would reallocate to the incumbent, limiting any spoiler's impact—analysis by BBC Verify found Peltola would still have won even if every vote for the other Daniel J Sullivan had gone to him. The seat began as a must-win toss-up but became surplus once Democrats secured enough seats nationally.
items.title: Mary Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Seat in Contested Midterm Race

items.summary: Nvidia announced that it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center chips to China, even though the company had won approval from the US government last year to sell a version of that model there. Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim chief executive officer, told analysts during an earnings call on Tuesday that the firm sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper data center products to China in the third quarter. However, she said its future guidance includes no such licensed Hopper shipments and confirmed it is ending them. Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments were being cut off. The move represents a notable shift for a company that has spent years seeking expanded business with Chinese customers. Jensen Huang, who was ousted as CEO last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, had been Nvidia's most vocal advocate for exporting chips to China. Huang departed after disclosing an affair with a woman now under investigation by the US government over potential ties to China's spy agency and possible help smuggling chips there; Beijing has denied attempting to spy on him. On Monday, the Trump administration moved to apply greater scrutiny to processor exports to several countries and to limit chip sales abroad when data center buyers plan to give Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. Nvidia had earlier pushed for permission to sell more advanced Blackwell chips to China; that request was never granted, but President Donald Trump approved the sale of Hopper processors known as H200s, which are two generations behind Nvidia's leading Rubin family of chips, reflecting the strong relationship Huang built with Trump. Harvey Jones, appointed Nvidia's first chair last week, said the board recognizes it is 'living in a world' where national security dynamics are reshaping its marketplace and that its next CEO must navigate those waters carefully. The company also announced forming a board committee focused on national security and export controls, boosted its sales forecast for next year, promised to improve access to critical supplies, and downplayed speculation about Huang's return. (Source: Bloomberg) Note the article does not state why Nvidia ended shipments beyond citing shifting national security dynamics; it attributes that framing to company leadership rather than providing independent detail on the decision itself.
items.title: Nvidia Halts Licensed Hopper Chip Shipments to China Despite Prior US Approval

items.summary: An artificial intelligence-based surveillance system is being tested in Chhattisgarh's Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve, where cameras mounted on towers 70-80 feet high are used to track elephants, tigers, and other wildlife while monitoring for poachers, timber smugglers, and encroachers. The system sends instant WhatsApp alerts to forest officials whenever an animal or suspicious human activity is detected. Director of the Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve Varun Jain stated that the pilot project operates across five forest ranges along the Odisha border — Kulhadighat, Indagaon, Risgaon, South Udanti, and Payalikhand North Udanti — areas characterized by dense forests and rugged terrain that function as important wildlife corridors but remain vulnerable to narcotics trafficking, illegal wildlife trade, timber smuggling, and encroachment. Because conventional mobile networks are unavailable in several remote forest locations, a dedicated point-to-point (P2P) wireless network will be established to provide connectivity; it will extend the 4G/5G network available in Mainpur to anti-poaching camps and forest outposts located 15-20 km away, enabling real-time video streaming and round-the-clock monitoring. The initiative follows increased conservation activity in previously inaccessible areas that had been difficult to reach due to Maoist presence; joint operations by the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and other security agencies have improved access to these regions. Each surveillance tower — including the AI camera, wireless connectivity system, tower structure, and associated civil works — is estimated to cost between ₹2.5 lakh and ₹3 lakh, and the units are portable so they can be relocated depending on operational requirements. Officials expect the system to help overcome a shortage of frontline forest personnel by strengthening surveillance and reducing gaps between patrols in sensitive locations, while also helping prevent human-wildlife conflict: when a tiger or other wild animal moves toward nearby settlements, alerts will reach mobile phones of concerned officers and field staff for quick response. The reserve already uses thermal drones for anti-poaching operations, wildlife and habitat monitoring, forest fire management, and encroachment detection, alongside satellite imagery and geospatial analysis using Google Earth Engine to track changes in forest cover and assess habitat restoration work. Over the past four years, the department reports reclaiming 956 hectares of forest land from encroachment and arresting more than 500 people allegedly involved in smuggling and poaching. The reserve has documented several wildlife species beyond tigers and elephants, including the Malabar pied hornbill, Indian giant squirrel, Indian flying squirrel, Indian paradise flycatcher, peregrine falcon, otters, and tricarinate hill turtle. State Correspondent Ritesh Mishra of Hindustan Times reported on the development from Raipur; figures such as tower heights, range names, network distances, costs, reclaimed hectares, arrests, and species are attributed to officials or department sources rather than independently verified here.
items.title: Chhattisgarh tests AI surveillance cameras in Udanti-Sitanadi Tiger Reserve to detect wildlife movement and poaching via WhatsApp alerts

items.summary: OpenAI announced that NATO is using up to 300 billion input and output tokens every month through its collaboration with the company, as part of an effort to strengthen the cybersecurity of allied networks. The partnership centers on OpenAI's work with NATO's Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to give the alliance's core institutions access to advanced cybersecurity models. These tools are being used for authorized security tasks, including reviewing software, investigating suspicious activity, identifying vulnerabilities, and developing and testing fixes. Dr Dylan Browne, General Manager of NCIA, stated that 'AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cyber security,' noting they accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed, and help defenders stay ahead of adversaries. He added that the experience would also allow NATO to understand token consumption, usage patterns, and the economics of AI models, supporting future cost optimization and procurement decisions. Beyond model access, OpenAI supported the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, which included a training program in which participants built, deployed, and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight. The collaboration extends beyond NATO: OpenAI has also provided its cybersecurity models to ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) and national cyber agencies in France, Germany, and Poland. Using these models, ENISA identified four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, publishing fixes for all four; a joint report by ENISA and CERT-EU found that 95 percent of the 88 potential issues assessed were confirmed as genuine. Poland's CERT Polska also used OpenAI models to identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, which researchers tested before disclosing them to the vendor, who released fixes. The announcement coincides with broader expansion at OpenAI, including recent introductions of GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday tasks. Sasha Baker, OpenAI's Head of National Security Policy, said the company intends to deepen its work with NATO and allied governments to strengthen the security of critical digital infrastructure, while continuing to help defenders identify vulnerabilities and develop fixes more quickly. items.summary: AI company Anthropic is preparing to debut on the stock market in an initial public offering (IPO) that could value it at $1.4 trillion (£1 trillion), making it one of the largest listings in history. The prospectus offers 825 million shares of Class A common stock at an initial price range of $70 to $78 per share, with the final price set for Wednesday and listing scheduled on Nasdaq in New York on Thursday. Although the shares carry voting rights, they combined represent only 49.9% of total voting power, meaning individual investors cannot force changes to how the company is run. Investor demand appears strong, with reports suggesting the offering is nearly six times oversubscribed, though this comes amid volatility in US markets and technology stocks generally. Retail investors in the UK can subscribe through AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro; minimum investments range from $250 (£189) at Robinhood and eToro to £250 at Hargreaves Lansdown and £1,000 at AJ Bell. Application deadlines are 1pm Wednesday for AJ Bell and 3pm for the others, though all platforms warn applications could close earlier without notice. Those who miss the offering can buy shares once trading begins on Nasdaq through additional platforms not participating in the deal. Investors may also gain exposure indirectly: UK funds such as Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage already hold stakes, Fidelity has investments available to US investors, and tracker or actively managed funds are expected to add Anthropic after listing. On risks, the prospectus contains 92 pages detailing potential threats, while recent technology-stock volatility adds market uncertainty. Governance concerns have been raised by The Guardian's financial editor Nils Pratley, who described the structure as representing an extraordinary concentration of power in a few individuals' hands. Jason Hollands, managing director of Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners (not participating in the IPO), cautioned that Anthropic remains capital-intensive and has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability, noting strong demand could lift prices initially but does not guarantee sustained gains.
items.title: Anthropic IPO: price, application process and risks for investors

items.summary: According to a report by Moneycontrol, Tata Sons sent the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) a letter dated October 6 seeking guidance on its listing obligations for upper-layer non-banking financial companies (NBFCs). The RBI responded late on November 16, clarifying that Tata Sons must comply with regulations applicable to upper-layer NBFCs, including the stock exchange listing requirement. In its correspondence, Tata Sons reportedly asked when the listing requirement would apply and what steps were needed for compliance, while informing the regulator of its intent to follow all applicable rules and initiate the required process. The RBI's response advised adherence to existing guidelines governing upper-layer NBFCs, which include mandatory listing provisions. Sources cited in the report say this clarification strengthened expectations that Tata Sons will pursue a stock exchange listing, though the precise deadline remains uncertain. A banker associated with the company reportedly noted that establishing an applicable timeline was among the objectives of the October letter. The RBI first classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer NBFC in September 2022, following scale-based regulations introduced in 2021; under this framework, companies in this category are generally required to list their shares within three years of classification. Tata Sons remained on the regulator's upper-layer NBFC list in September 2023 and was again included in its January 16, 2025 list while acknowledging its application to surrender its NBFC registration; at that time, the RBI clarified that the classification would remain subject to the outcome of the deregistration request, which was under examination. The November clarification has renewed attention on Tata Sons' regulatory obligations, with the central question now focusing on the listing deadline and how existing rules apply to the company's circumstances. All details are drawn from a single report by Moneycontrol citing unnamed sources; no official statement or confirmation from the RBI or Tata Sons is provided in the source material.
items.title: RBI Clarifies Tata Sons Must List as Upper-Layer NBFC; Timeline Still Unclear

items.summary: Vartika Singh, who leads strategic AI at Nvidia, published a personal tribute on LinkedIn to CEO Jensen Huang. The post appeared days after Huang resigned amid national security concerns raised by his extramarital affair and ongoing investigations. Singh described nearly eight years of working with him, stating she had never worked for anyone like him and doubted she ever would. She emphasized that she could speak only to what she personally witnessed. Her most personal account concerned her sister Shilpi, who has been fighting brain cancer. When Shilpi's condition worsened during a visit to California, the family faced devastating medical decisions and overwhelming hospital expenses, along with the possibility of losing her far from home. Singh said Huang made time for the family despite his heavy workload, helped them through what seemed an impossible situation, and met her sister—a meeting she photographed as a keepsake for life. He reportedly told her he was proud of her and urged her to treasure the time with her sister; that moment, she wrote, taught her something about leadership that professional experience never could. Singh also described Huang's less visible side, noting she had watched him back researchers, founders, and startups when few others would, including struggling companies and ideas that seemed too early—some of which might not exist without his time, attention, and Nvidia's resources. She credited him with long-term thinking, saying it sometimes took her years to grasp implications he saw almost immediately, and said his guidance helped her through difficult organizational transitions at Nvidia. Reflecting on the future, she wrote that leadership changes and new chapters begin, but the influence of someone who shaped so many people and ideas outlasts any title; she ended with thanks for his guidance, backing of people and ideas early, and what she called his humanity. Of her own future she wrote only that she does not know what comes next. Her post is one of several tributes from Nvidia staff. More than 160,000 people have signed a petition seeking Huang's return as CEO, with tech executives, employees, and investors backing him despite ongoing investigations. Some outlets covering her post also reported critical accounts from inside the company; one separate report cited employees describing harsh verbal criticism and outbursts.
items.title: Nvidia Employee Vartika Singh Tributes Jensen Huang Before His Exit

items.summary: The Government of Andhra Pradesh amended its Semiconductor & Display Fab Policy 4.0 on November 16, 2026 (G.O.Ms.No.87) so it aligns with the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM Semicon 2.0). Under the amendment, the State matches 100% of the Centre's capital support for silicon fabs, display fabs and chip packaging projects. With this top-up, a silicon fab approved under Semicon 2.0 can receive combined support equal to 80% of its eligible capital cost: 40% from the Government of India and 40% from Andhra Pradesh. Compound semiconductor, photonics, sensor, discrete and display fabs, plus advanced packaging units, qualify for 70%, while legacy packaging units get 50%. In comparing with other states, AP's 80% for silicon fabs is higher than Odisha (65%), Tamil Nadu (65%), Uttar Pradesh (60%), Madhya Pradesh (60%) and Gujarat (56%). Minister Nara Lokesh stated in a Wednesday release: "Andhra Pradesh wants to be the place where India builds its chips, from design to fab to packaging." He added that by matching Centre support rupee for rupee, offering investors one window, and building needed talent, AP is making it simpler and cheaper than anywhere else. The amended policy covers all 10 Semicon 2.0 categories under six pillars: design, machines and materials, fabs, packaging, research and development, and talent. For chip design the State adds 50% of the Centre's support; commercial design start-ups can receive combined seed funding of up to ₹22.5 crore, including up to ₹7.5 crore from the State. Under a deployment-linked incentive, the State adds 4.5% of net sales on top of the Centre's 9%, bringing the total to 13.5%; this is capped at ₹45 crore per application and ₹180 crore per company. For machines and materials, the State adds 18% of capital cost on top of the Centre's 30%, for combined support of 48%, plus the Centre's production-linked incentive. Assembly, testing, marking and packaging (ATMP) and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) units get 100% of the Centre's capital support matched by the State. For R&D and talent projects, the State provides 25% of eligible project cost, with combined Centre and State support capped at 75%. Total State incentives are capped at 50% of eligible fixed capital investment, while support from all sources is capped at 90%. The State's share is released after each tranche from the Centre, on the same schedule. AP plans a dedicated Semiconductor Park of about 5,000 acres at Tirupati as a manufacturing and supplier cluster for the full value chain; it will be run by a public-private park company with an investor-led board that has up to three government nominees, offering developed land, shared industrial cleanrooms, high-voltage power with redundancy, ultrapure water, natural gas and specialty gases, effluent treatment and water recycling, testing labs, logistics, and research and training centres on site. The AP Semiconductor Growth & Innovation Council (APSGIC) will serve as a single point of contact for investors; it has an Oversight Council chaired by the Chief Minister and a CEO-led Apex Committee that appraises projects, recommends State incentives, and drives clearances, land, power, water and coordination with ISM and the Union Ministry of Electronics and IT. The AP Semiconductor Research & Innovation Centre (AP-SRIC) will be a not-for-profit company with independent professional management; it starts at IIT Tirupati and later moves to the Park, with photonics as its first focus. The AP Semiconductor Training & Capacity Building Centre (AP-STCC) is a training centre inside the Park, with curricula designed with industry and AP universities; companies receive a training subsidy of ₹10,000 per trainee per month for six months. Mega projects (₹1,000 crore to ₹5,000 crore) and ultra-mega projects (above ₹5,000 crore) can get tailor-made packages decided case by case by the State Investment Promotion Board chaired by the Chief Minister. Projects not under Semicon 2.0 may receive a power subsidy of ₹3 per unit for five years from commercial production, along with incentives under AP's industrial or electronics policies. The policy is valid for five years until replaced by a new one; amendments apply immediately and benefits already granted are protected, while operating guidelines on eligibility, appraisal and disbursement will be notified separately. Published November 18, 2026.
items.title: Andhra Pradesh Amends Semiconductor Policy to Match Centre Support and Offer Up to 80% Capital Incentives

items.summary: Every monsoon in Darjeeling, the Himalayan salamander emerges from the forest floor to breed in small ponds known locally as pokhris. Males and females engage in a courtship dance before fertilized eggs are laid on half-submerged vegetation; larvae hatch into the water over two weeks, develop lungs, adopt a terrestrial lifestyle, and later return to their birth ponds once sexually mature. Worldwide there are about 830 salamander species, predominantly found in North America, Europe, and Asia, while India hosts only two. The Himalayan salamander (Tylototriton himalayanus), also called the Himalayan crocodile newt, occurs in eastern Nepal, the Darjeeling Himalayas, and western Bhutan; it has a brown body with a blunt snout and rows of knobby warts along its back that may release toxins when disturbed. Adults are found near water bodies from roughly late April to early October and spend the rest of the year on land under rocks or logs. The Manipuri newt (Tylototriton zaimeng), also known as the Zaimeng newt, was described only in 2023; it has a broad head, rounded snout, short limbs, brown skin with orange-yellow markings on the head, back, sides, palms, and soles, and is restricted to the Khongtheng mountain range in Manipur, where it was first found at Zaimeng lake and surrounding mountain lakes and ponds. The Himalayan salamander is classified as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List; scientists who described the Manipuri newt suggested the same category for it because of its highly restricted range. Both species receive the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Salamanders' wetland habitats are shrinking rapidly due to drainage for housing and tourism and pollution from wastewater; roads cut across migration routes causing accidental roadkill; only a small fraction of current habitat lies within protected areas while most remaining habitat occurs on private land and tea estates. Barkha Subba, conservation scientist and 2026 Whitley Award winner, told Mongabay-India in April 2026: "Meeting a salamander feels like meeting a messenger from deep evolutionary time — a reminder of how long nature has endured and how quickly we can lose it." items.summary: In a housing society in West Goregaon, Mr. Jayaswal owns flat D-101 and Mrs. Nalawade owns flat D-201 within the four-wing (A, B, C, D) complex. The society originally had 40 members before an approved redevelopment plan raised membership to 215; under that plan only two flats of 1300 sq.ft each were built in the D wing, both owned by Jayaswal and Nalawade. Redevelopment was completed in 2016, and on May 20, 2018 the society asked flat owners to begin paying maintenance charges. From 2018 through 2022 each owner paid Rs 7,867 monthly; from 2022 onward the society raised Jayaswal's charge to Rs 27,166 and Nalawade's to Rs 29,266, arguing that maintaining the D wing cost more. The owners refused, contending maintenance should be calculated per flat rather than per wing, and also claimed that since July 2022 the society had withdrawn security and housekeeping services for their flats. On November 3, 2026 they won an interim case at the Maharashtra State Co-Operative Appellate Court, which ordered the society to stop collecting the enhanced amount until the dispute is resolved. Advocate Vishal Gehrana of Karanjawala & Company told ET Wealth Online that a nearly fourfold increase naturally raises questions about how the new figure was calculated and that these two members' challenge had merit at the interim stage. He said the society decided to recalculate maintenance on a wing-wise basis but failed to follow through with safeguards it had promised residents, including verification of calculations, consideration of objections before implementation, appointment of an independent Chartered Accountant, display of figures on the notice board, and hearing member concerns before finalizing revised billing. Gehrana noted that although a general body has broad authority over day-to-day affairs, this power is not unlimited; he cited the Bombay High Court's Venus Co-operative housing society ruling holding that a majority cannot use its voting power to justify an arbitrary or unreasonable demand on others. The order remains interim: the court did not declare wing-wise maintenance unlawful nor finally hold the revised charges illegal. On the record, A wing has 82 flats, B wing has 55 flats, C wing has 76 flats, and D wing has only 2 flats; it is admitted that after redevelopment these four wings were constructed by the builder. The society claimed a majority vote at an AGM dated September 30, 2018 led to a resolution passed under agenda No.4 in the AGM dated March 27, 2022, and argued this majority cannot be challenged by two members. However, the court found no copy of minutes showing that AGM approved revising maintenance; instead those minutes show the secretary proposed recalculating charges after considering actual expenses per unit, appointing a Chartered Accountant to confirm calculations, displaying them on the notice board, and finalizing revised billing only after hearing member objections. The society never held an AGM or SGM to discuss the CA-confirmed figures nor considered member objections before finalizing rates. Although the society alleged that its managing committee unanimously approved the revised calculations at a meeting on May 20, 2022, it produced no such resolution; in a co-operative society any maintenance increase must be approved by the general body, and the managing committee cannot take policy decisions without that approval. The court observed that imposing revised charges directly from July 1, 2022 was against the object of the Co-operative Act, and under Model Byelaws 2014 maintenance should be charged per flat or unit rather than wing-wise. When asked how D wing incurred higher costs, the society cited a separate water connection, electricity connection, a lift for only two flats, and use of the common compound as personal space; the court rejected these reasons as consistent with the redevelopment plan and not extraordinary facilities enjoyed by the two owners. The court held that since constructing four wings with different flat counts was the society's own decision, it could not blame the disputants for using lift, water, and electricity services sized to only two flats, nor be allowed to charge exorbitant maintenance on D wing flats.
items.title: Maharashtra Co-Operative Appellate Court halts wing-wise maintenance hike for two Goregaon flat owners

items.summary: This document is a collection of reader letters responding to articles published in Scroll's EcoIndia section and elsewhere. One letter questions the decision to include an article about the emerging Jewish community in Andhra Pradesh, describing it as lacking literary or culinary value and suggesting it was a thinly veiled attempt at seeding Jewish ancestry; the writer also expresses doubt that the publication edited the piece and raises concerns about Israel's treatment of Palestinians before stating their ability to read Scroll with trust is broken. Another letter addresses how Rabindranath Tagore should be judged by Bangladeshis, arguing that his appeal lies in the universality of his art rather than modernity or communal identity, noting he never considered himself Hindu or Muslim but a human being who found unity amid diversity; this writer observes that whether Muslim-majority Bangladesh tolerates the cultural and spiritual dominance of a Hindu Tagore will determine his fate there. A third letter contends that Tagore has received more privilege than other Bengali poets and notes he opposed the establishment of Dhaka University following the Partition of Bengal, arguing against blind worship of him. A fourth letter discusses votebank politics in India, comparing how secular and Left parties relied on upper-caste and lower-caste Muslim support to how middle-class Hindus are treated by the Bharatiya Janata Party; the writer argues these groups remain trapped with identity and ideology and that both Hindus and Muslims will not prosper unless they confront this dynamic. A fifth letter from a 78-year-old praises election conduct, honoring Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha for setting aside Indira Gandhi's election and TN Seshan as outstanding stalwarts of independent India. Another comment references the SIR exercise in Karnataka, suggesting banks should adopt similar practices while noting many people hold multiple bank accounts; this is followed by a separate remark calling for the Supreme Court to stop centralized election software. A further letter criticizes the conduct of the Supreme Court and Chief Election Commissioner over millions of eligible voters being deprived of their rights during an election where judges reportedly only said vote next time, urging a mass movement against errant judges. The final letter responds positively to an EcoIndia episode on reviving India's repair culture to curb e-waste; it argues that forcing companies to make phones in particular ways might kill innovation or be difficult to enforce technically, and instead suggests requiring original spare parts sold openly like car service parts, starting with a battery buyback mandate for smartphones and incentives such as tax cuts for modular designs like Fairphones. The document contains no figures beyond the age of one letter's writer (78) and references to millions of eligible voters being deprived of their rights.
items.title: Readers' comments on Tagore, Jewish community cuisine, votebank politics and election conduct
