The article opens by noting that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, and his public admission of being unfaithful to wife Lori Mills. While this drew attention to the personal life of a billionaire ranking 16th on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index with an estimated net worth of $130 billion, it also spotlighted the financial scale of high-profile divorces. The piece then surveys five such settlements.

Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates separated in May 2021 after nearly 27 years of marriage. NDTV Profit reported that Melinda received more than $2 billion in shares, though exact terms remain undisclosed. In 2024 she announced leaving the Gates Foundation under an agreement worth $12.5 billion for her philanthropic work; although this was not part of a publicly confirmed divorce settlement, reports put the combined value of their financial arrangements at more than $14.5 billion. The couple agreed to divide marital assets, and Melinda did not seek spousal support.

Jeff Bezos divorced MacKenzie Scott in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage. As part of the settlement, Scott received about 4% of Amazon's total outstanding shares — 19.7 million shares valued at approximately $38.3 billion at the time. Bezos retained a 12% stake and control over the voting rights attached to the transferred shares. Scott later committed through the Giving Pledge to donate at least half of her wealth to charity; the settlement was notable for transferring a substantial company stake rather than being limited to cash.

French-American art dealer Alec Wildenstein married Jocelyn in 1978 and divorced in 1999 after 21 years. Jocelyn reportedly received an initial $2.5 billion, followed by annual payments of $100 million for 13 years, bringing the combined reported settlement to approximately $3.8 billion. Wildenstein died in 2008.

Rupert Murdoch divorced journalist Anna Murdoch in 1999 after nearly three decades of marriage and had three children together. Their settlement was widely reported at $1.7 billion, much associated with News Corporation shares, though exact terms were never disclosed and the figure has been questioned; it was structured to protect his control over his business empire.

Bill Gross, co-founder of Pacific Investment Management Company (PIMCO), married Sue Gross in 1985. They separated in 2016 after more than three decades when Sue filed for divorce in November that year. She reportedly received assets worth $1.3 billion, including a $36 million property in Laguna Beach and half of the couple's art collection.

The article concludes that these divorces — spanning company shares, investment assets, and court awards — demonstrate how high-profile separations carry significant financial consequences, even as several exact terms remain private. The piece is written by Swati Gandhi, a digital journalist with over four years' experience covering international and geopolitical issues for Business Standard and Live Mint.
items.title: Five of the world's most expensive billionaire divorce settlements

items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Tuesday stayed investigations into three cases against 10 persons accused of fraudulently using Form 7s of the Election Commission to delete Muslim voters during a special intensive revision of electoral rolls, per Bar and Bench. Form 7 is used to object to inclusion or seek deletion of names from an electoral roll. The FIRs were filed after complainants alleged that Form 7s had been submitted in bulk based on false information, forged signatures, and impersonation to remove eligible electors, mainly Muslims, from voter lists. In October, the court had stayed probes in two other similar cases; Tuesday's order extended the stay to three more cases involving 10 accused persons. The Congress-led state government opposed the petitions seeking a stay, contending that the right to vote is extremely valuable and that fake or forged forms cannot be allowed. Petitioners argued instead that booth-level agents are entitled to file Form 7s on behalf of political parties during electoral roll preparation and revision, complementing the Election Commission's booth level officers, and that correctness should be examined by the electoral registration officer. The court directed the poll panel to place materials relating to decisions taken on Form 7 use on record, observing that the statutory inquiry into their correctness under the 1960 Registration of Electors Rules must first be completed before any police investigation is warranted. That same rules framework provides for imprisonment of up to one year, a fine, or both, for knowingly making a false written declaration; the bench noted these provisions while examining scrutiny and hearing procedures. The stay thus defers criminal action pending completion of that inquiry. This case sits within a broader national revision exercise: its first phase ran in Bihar in 2025, was extended to 12 states and Union Territories in late 2025 and the first half of 2026 as a second phase, and a third phase is underway across 19 states and Union Territories. Since it began, concerns have been raised that revision could eliminate genuine voters or shape electoral outcomes; Scroll reported on these worries. In May, the Supreme Court upheld the legality of the revision but said it does not permit the Election Commission to decide whether a person is an Indian citizen. Despite this, Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states have cited the SIR to deny ration cards to those eliminated from rolls, and in some cases police denied passport renewal permission. Since October 2, nationwide protests calling for resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have been held over concerns about the Commission's functioning and alleged irregularities in roll revision.
items.title: Karnataka HC stays police probe in three Form 7 fraud cases over Muslim voter deletions
